editorial:
Ever wonder how a regular janitor could trick the entire world? You get to follow Paul Kroll, a guy starting from the bottom in Chicago who has a massive chip on his shoulder and a genius for lying. He doesn't want a simple life; he wants power and money. After scamming his way back to Sweden, he uses his smooth talking and fake promises to take over the matchstick industry. It feels like a classic climb-to-the-top story where you almost root for the bad guy because he is just so good at playing the game.

The acting is surprisingly sharp for an old film, and the way the plot moves from a small city to an international stage keeps you interested. While some parts might feel a bit slow compared to modern movies, the tension builds up nicely as his lies get bigger and harder to manage. If you enjoy seeing a con artist get away with everything until the very end, you will love this.
endingExplained: The movie ends when the house of cards finally falls apart. After years of pretending to be a billionaire and controlling the match market, Paul's lies catch up to him. The world discovers his huge debts and fake accounts. Instead of facing the shame of a public trial and losing everything, he takes his own life. It is a sad but fitting end for a man who spent his whole life pretending to be someone he wasn't.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves stories about scammers and huge financial crashes.
